summary: The note traces Southern Italian cuisine through successive historical eras, from Greek settlement and Roman influence through Arab, Norman, Hohenstaufen and Spanish rule to modern dishes. It highlights how each culture contributed ingredients and techniques, how poverty produced cucina povera, and how recent decades have seen a revival through food festivals and the Slow Food movement.
one_line: A chronological survey of how Greek, Roman, Arab, Norman, Spanish and modern influences shaped Southern Italian cuisine and its current revival.
key_facts: Greeks settled Southern Italy (Magna Graecia) and brought olive trees and vines, establishing olive oil and wine traditions.
The Greeks seasoned banquet dishes with "garos," a fermented fish sauce considered a predecessor of anchovy paste.
In the first century A.D. the Romans made wheat a staple, leading to breads and a precursor to pasta.
Apicius, author of the cookbook "De Re Coquinaria," described dishes akin to minestra (soup) and patina (pie).
Around the ninth century the Arabs introduced rice, saffron and citrus fruits to Sicily, along with sweet and sour flavors, and fostered dried pasta because of its long shelf life.
The Normans arrived in the 11th century and the Hohenstaufen dynasty in the 12th, bringing feudalism; Palermo's court under Emperor Frederick II mixed Norman, Germanic, Arab and Greek influences.
Under Spanish domination from the late 15th century, the Columbian Exchange introduced tomatoes, peppers, potatoes and maize to Southern Italy.
By the 17th century tomatoes were common in dishes such as pasta al pomodoro, and pizza was emerging in Naples.
Pizza Margherita was created in 1889 with tomato, mozzarella and basil, representing the colors of the Italian flag and Italian unification.
Ragù was born in the courts of the Bourbon kings as a meat-based aristocratic sauce and later spread across all social levels.

Cucina povera, 'the poor kitchen,' arose from 20th-century economic hardship and uses simple, local, seasonal ingredients; pasta con le sarde (sardines, wild fennel, pine nuts, raisins) is an example.
Thousands of sagre (food festivals) are held annually, each dedicated to a local dish or ingredient.
Carla Capalbo and Vincenzo Buonassisi are named as chefs and food historians who document ancient recipes.
The Slow Food movement originated in Italy and has a passionate following in the South, alongside a push for sustainable agriculture and biodiversity.
